conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to be sure you’re getting the support you need.  

Today we’ll use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days, and it includes a gentle question about self-harm so we can keep you safe.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and the clinical team; there are no right or wrong answers, and you can pause any time. We’ll go through ten questions together—I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[sighs softly, eyes on the floor]  
I’ve tried—my partner will show me a silly meme or make a joke—but mostly I just force a little smile. Nothing feels genuinely funny right now. It’s like the laughter is stuck somewhere behind all the worry and exhaustion.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow head-shake]  
No… not really. I can’t remember actually laughing this week. Even when my sister sent that video of the cat sliding off the counter, I just stared at it. Everyone else was cracking up, but I felt nothing—just flat, like the joy part is broken.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice small]  
Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but lately even those feel like chores. Yesterday my mom offered to watch the baby so I could go get my nails done, and I just felt… nothing. I went anyway, sat there the whole time thinking, “Why doesn’t this feel fun anymore?”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes tear up, voice wavers]  
All the time. Yesterday he wouldn’t latch and I kept thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like if I were a better mom he’d eat easily. When he cries for more than a few minutes I’m sure it’s my fault for not knowing what he needs. I keep replaying every little thing and finding ways it could’ve been better if I just tried harder.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly imagine he stopped breathing, or I’ll picture myself dropping him, and my heart starts racing. Nothing triggered it—he’s right there, pink and wiggly—but I can’t shake the dread. Sometimes I have to put him in the crib for a second and pace the hallway just to catch my breath.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses palms together]  
Yes… a few nights this week I woke up suddenly and my heart was pounding so hard I thought something awful must be happening. The room felt heavy, like I couldn’t get enough air, even though the baby was asleep and nothing was wrong. It passes after a bit, but in that moment I’m terrified and I don’t know why.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]  
Most days, honestly. I’ll be trying to fold laundry while he naps and suddenly feel like the pile is towering over me—like every tiny task is just too much. I’ll stand in the kitchen staring at the bottles that need washing and feel this tightness in my chest, thinking, “How am I supposed to keep doing all of this?” I manage, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly]  
Yeah… even when the baby’s finally down, my mind just keeps spinning. I lie there replaying everything I might’ve messed up—did I burp him long enough, did I snap at my partner—and the sadness feels like this heavy blanket I can’t push off. Some nights I watch the clock slide past two, then three, and I’m still wide-awake with this knot in my chest.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard]  
Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around—even when the baby smiles or someone says something nice, the happy moment feels thin and fades fast. I wake up already feeling low, and by evening it’s like I’m dragging the sadness from room to room.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, eyes welling]  
Yeah… a few times this week. Two nights ago I was rocking him at 3 a.m. and I just started sobbing—quietly, so I wouldn’t wake him. It wasn’t about any one thing; it was everything piling up. The tears come out of nowhere sometimes, and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I get exhausted and overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my son.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughter and excitement feel distant, daily tasks seem insurmountable, and a constant gray cloud of sadness follows you even when you try to enjoy your baby. Despite your deep wish to feel better and parent well, you're battling relentless worry, sudden panic, and nightly tears, yet you bravely continue to care for your son and reach out for help.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>"Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia), matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame ("all the time") with specific recent examples and rumination, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, unprovoked anxious thoughts about infant safety and physical symptoms of panic, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden night-time panic attacks with palpitations, breathlessness, and intense fear without cause, matching "Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by persistent sadness and rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with inability to feel sustained joy, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week, including a specific incident during night feeding, indicating crying "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 26 places you well above the high-risk cutoff of 13, indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse core symptoms consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</medi>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, recurrent thoughts of inadequacy as a mother, psychomotor agitation (pacing), fatigue, insomnia, and distress that impairs daily functioning. Anxiety symptoms (Q4, Q5) are also prominent and commonly co-occur in the postpartum period. No self-harm ideation is present, reducing immediate safety risk yet not diminishing the clinical urgency of treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or psychiatrist for comprehensive evaluation
3. Consider evidence-based treatments such as <med>interpersonal psychotherapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> for postpartum depression
4. Discuss with your provider whether an <med>SSRI antidepressant</med> compatible with breastfeeding might be appropriate
5. Enlist practical support-ask trusted family or friends to help with household tasks, meals, or night shifts so you can rest
6. Use brief self-care strategies: 10-minute outdoor walks, balanced snacks, and breathing exercises when the baby sleeps
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress after starting treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood (non-diagnostic)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding parenting adequacy  
- Chronic anxiety, panic attacks (no clear triggers), intrusive fears of infant harm  
- Sleep disturbance driven by rumination, not infant needs  
- Overwhelm, sense of inability to cope with routine tasks  

Pattern  
Consistent with elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms of postpartum onset; no current self-harm ideation (explicitly denied).

Risk indicators  
– Loss of pleasure and pervasive sadness >2 wk  
– Guilt/cognitive self-attack  
– Panic episodes  
– Functional impairment (household tasks, social withdrawal)  
– No suicidal thoughts (safety factor)

Summary  
Patient screens positive for probable postpartum depression ± anxiety; high distress, functional impact, no self-harm intent. Recommend formal clinical evaluation for diagnosis and treatment planning.
